sections.text: अस्माकं तु विशिष्टा ये तान्निबोध द्विजोत्तम।
Know also, O best among the twice-born! the names of those who are the most distinguished amongst ourselves, the leaders of my army; these I name to thee for thy information.
Thyself and Bhishma, and Karna and also Kripa, the victorious in war, Asvatthama, Vikarna, and also Bhurisrava, the son of Somadatta.
अन्ये च बहवः शूरा मदर्थे त्यक्तजीविताः।
And also many other heroes who are ready to give up their lives for my sake, armed with various weapons and missiles, all well-skilled in battle.

We had been discussing Chapter 1, Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the Yoga of Arjunas Grief. As we discussed before, this is a chapter which gives us the context for the dialogue between Arjuna and Krishna. Bhagavad Gita is part of the Prasthana Trayi, one of the three legs of our philosophy: the Upanishads, Brahma Sutra, and Bhagavad Gita.
Bhagavad Gita has a unique place, as we have discussed, it is not only a Shruti because it reveals the Brahma Vidya, but it is also applicable for day-to-day living and social order. Therefore it is also considered Smriti. In that context, were seeing Chapter 1 as a study in how different people react to the same situation.
We started this Bhagavad Gita with Dhritarashtras query to Sanjaya: Whats happening at the battlefield? Dharmakshetra, Kurukshetra, Mamakaha, Pandavaschain. The very first thing we notice is how Dhritarashtra thinks, this world is divided into mine and yours, mine and the rest of the world. Mamakaha, mine, and Pandavas. This is the central issue we deal with in philosophy: in our Advaita philosophy, the root cause of all our problems is duality.
This duality, I as an island by myself, and the world out there, creates friction between I and the world. The very first indication, the first word, tells us where we stand. We are in the Dhrutrastra Sthiti.
We see this world as I, mine and rest. And then as we further go into the chapter we see Sanjays narration. Sanjaya starts his narration with what is Duryodhan doing? So we are seeing now the world from Duryodhans perspective, same situation.
The two armies are facing each other. War is about to be started. We all know the background of why they are there very elaborately.
The Mahabharata describes what happened before we came to this point of two armies facing each other. Now Duryodhana is looking at the situation. He sees it from a very different perspective: Is this winnable or not? Am I in a winning position or a losing position? The same situation, as well see further in the chapter, Arjuna looks at very differently.
He looks at it as whether its right or wrong to be here. So it gives us various perspectives on how we look at our lives. When we face any situation, depending on our own mental condition, we look at it that way.
The scriptures are nothing but the mirror of our mind. Every time we read the scriptures, we see our own reflection in it. So we have seen that Sanjaya first says that, looking at the Pandava army, Raja Duryodhana went to Drona and told him thus.
And then he described what he told Drona. First of all, as we know, the commander-in-chief on the Kaurava side was Bheeshma; on the Pandava side, Drishtadyumna, Drupadas son. So if Duryodhana had any question, doubt, or concern, he should have gone to Bheeshma and said, Lets make sure we are in a winning position. But instead, he goes to Drona, his teacher.
It seems he felt there was a soft spot. Drona is as powerful as Bheeshma and Arjuna in terms of his prowess in warfare. But he knew that he has soft spot for his students.
Every teacher has soft spot for his or her best student. Arjuna was Dronas best student. Not only that, all other people who are the great warriors on the other side are Dronas student.
So he is now questioning whether he will be at his best when Drona fights this war. It seems therefore he goes to Drona and tells him look at the army on the Pandava side. It is commanded by an able commander like Drishtadyumna, your wise student.
Then he said all of them are your students, they know as much as you know, or you are the one who trained them. So we have seen in the first six verses he describes who are on the Pandava side. Then the next six verses, he describes who are on our side.
But now he is putting it in a way which seems slightly odd: he says Asmakam tu Vishishta ye Tanibodha Dvijottama. He addresses Drona as Dvijottama, best among Brahmins. But he is not here as a Brahmin; here he is a warrior. Drona, even though he was born a Brahmin, spent his life in the art of warfare and became the greatest teacher.
Thats why Bhishma actually replaced Kripacharya, who was supposed to be the Raj Guru, he realized that Drona is a better teacher for his grandchildren, all Kauravas and Pandavas. So Drona was the best. But here Duryodhana goes to him and says, Oh, best among the Brahmins. It seems like a compliment, but its a backhanded compliment, at the end of the day, youre a Brahmin.
And Brahmins are known to be softer; they cant tolerate physical or mental torture or agonies. Theres a story in Mahabharata about Karna. Karna goes to Parashuram because he wanted to learn.
He disguised himself as a Brahmin, because Parashuram wouldnt teach anyone but Brahmins, Parashuram had taken a vow to wipe out all Kshatriyas from this planet. So Karna disguised himself, and it went well. But one day, a worm was biting Karnas thigh and he started bleeding.
His teacher was sleeping with his head on Karnas lap. The blood started going under Parashurams head. He felt this hot blood, woke up, and realized what had happened.
He said, You are not a Brahmin. You cannot be a Brahmin if you can tolerate that much pain without moving. As we see from this story, Brahmins are known to be softer. Dvijottama, essentially calling him a soft person. So hes saying: Asmakam tu Vishishta, be aware that even on our side, the warriors are not ordinary; they are better than normal. Nayaka Mama Sainyasya, the leaders in my army.
See the words, mama, mamakaha, on one side. That is the root cause of my problems. Nayaka Mama Sainyasya Sanjnartham Tan Bravimi Te, Im going to enumerate who the special leaders in our army are. There was no reason whatsoever for Drona to know any of this.
He already knew, and it wasnt even Dronas business to worry about. He had his own position and duties. Bhishma was the one who had to worry about who is where.
But he is telling Drona, he seems to be suffering from anxiety about whether this war is winnable or not. Hes getting a little worried. This is what happens when we go for a presentation and we know there are three national firms were competing against.
We start looking at our strong points: Look, our strong point is that we are local, then we have this, and we have that. This shows our anxiety, how are we going to win this thing when we are fighting against a mightier competitor? So here he is enumerating who are on his side to Drona, which shows his anxiety about whether the war is winnable or not, even though he had the larger army. It also tells us that acquiring and accomplishing more things will not make us more secure, which is how we live our lives. The more Ill acquire, the more secure I will be; the larger the bank balance, the more my retirement will be secured. Its actually the other way around. The more I acquire and accomplish, the more insecure I become, because my expectations from life grow more and more.
I start relying on my accomplishments and achievements, and I see a long way to go to be perfect. I was talking to my investment advisors: What is the guarantee that you will be able to protect my nest egg 20 years from now? There are no guarantees. If I never had that much money to worry about 20 years from now, who worries? Whatever it is, but because at least something that I worry about.
So more I acquire, more insecure I become. Thats the lesson we learn from this. So hes now insecure and now he says Im going to enumerate what are our assets.
These are our assets. What is our liability? Our liability is all your students on this side. But at the same token our assets.
Bhavan, starting with you, you are one of my assets. Bhavan Bhishmas cha, yourself and Bhishma, and also Karna and Kripa, Samatinjaya. Duryodhana adds an adjective to Kripacharya: Samatinjaya, victorious in war. Dronacharya knew who Kripacharya was, his brother-in-law who had been replaced by Drona as teacher by Bhishma. Now Duryodhana is calling him the victorious one. This shows Duryodhanas anxiety and his attempt to make Dronacharya feel more loyal and faithful to him.
Then he lists Ashvatthama, Dronas son, Vikarna, and Somadattas son. So he enumerated these people starting from you, Drona. He wanted to make him feel like you are important.
Just make sure that your loyalty is not divided between Pandavas and us. Because your students are there. Your best student is on other side.
But I consider you as my asset. Then he continues and says, a Nyecha Baha vah Suraha, Madharte Takta, Jeevi taha. There are many others, great warriors.
They are willing to give their lives for me. So its all about me. You can see in these verses.
Theres more mama in it than anything else. Hes not describing anything which is of value to Drona. Hes not describing any strategy.
Lets make sure that we all understood what our game plan is. Hes just simply saying, look how we are in a better situation. Because I am at the center of this and everybody is fighting for me.
They are ready to give their lives for me. Nana, Sastra, Prahananah, Sarvey, Yudda, Vishaaradaha. Theyre all expert in weapons of various kinds and missiles.
Something which you throw is a Prahana, a pariyaptam. So this verse in verse 10 is important to understand. Aparyaptam tad asmakam balam Bhishma abhiraksitam, paryaptam tvidam etesham balam Bhima abhiraksitam. Now Duryodhana gives his conclusion after evaluating who is on the Pandavas side and who is on our side. There are two interpretations here.
One interpretation: Aparyaptam, our army seems unlimited, because its so huge and protected by Bhishma, it seems plenty. Paryaptam tvidam etesham balam, and the army protected by Bhima seems limited, not large enough. We are in a winning situation. Im not exactly sure why Duryodhana names Bhima instead of Dhrishtadyumna who was the actual commander, but Bhima.
The simple explanation is that Duryodhanas direct rival is Bhima, because both were mace warriors. Everyone who reads Bhagavad Gita comes up with their own interpretation. Different Acharyas who follow Advaita, Vishishta Advaita, or Dvaita philosophy, all of them have looked at Bhagavad Gita and reached their own conclusions.
Even though the Dhyana Shloka says Advaita Amruta Varshini Ashtadasa Adhyayini, clearly describing it as the showerer of Advaita philosophy, we still have these different interpretations. So here is one way to look at this verse. If Duryodhana feels this is a winnable situation, he will say we have an unlimited army.
The 11 akshauhinis versus 7 is the perfect combination for victory.

In these verses, Duryodhana addresses Drona as Dvijottama, best among the twice-born Brahmins. Though this sounds like a compliment, its actually a subtle accusation: Remember, youre just a Brahmin, soft by nature, with divided loyalties to your students on both sides. Notice how Duryodhana lists his own generals, Bhavan (yourself), Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Ashwatthama, Vikarna, Somadatta, not to strategize, but to reassure himself. He says these warriors are ready to give their lives madarthe, for my sake. The repeated use of mama (mine) reveals his self-centered view of the entire conflict.
Reflect on your own patterns of seeking reassurance when facing challenges. Do you enumerate your assets to others when youre actually trying to convince yourself? Do you subtly question the loyalty of those around you, revealing your own insecurity rather than any real deficiency in them? Duryodhana had eleven akshauhinis, a massive army, yet couldnt feel secure. This teaches us that acquiring more accomplishments, wealth, or allies doesnt bring lasting security. In fact, More I acquire, more insecure I become, because my expectations from life become more and more.
This week, notice where youre seeking external validation for decisions youve already made internally. When you find yourself listing your strengths or resources to others, pause and ask: Am I strategizing, or am I managing my own anxiety? The difference matters. True confidence comes not from counting whats on your side, but from knowing your cause is aligned with dharma.
